column2: (a) A function assigns exactly one output to each input in its domain; its range is the set of attained outputs. (b) Its graph is {(x,f(x))}. (c) Use the vertical-line test.
column3: For every admitted x, plot just the point whose height is f(x). A vertical line x=a can therefore meet the graph at at most one point.
column4: Domain concerns allowed inputs, while range concerns outputs actually produced, not all numbers in a possible codomain.

column2: Verbal, numerical, graphical, and algebraic representations.
column3: For a $2-per-item cost: verbally state the unit price; numerically list (0,0),(1,2),(2,4); graph those points; algebraically write C(n)=2n for nonnegative integers n.
column4: All four describe the same input-output relationship but emphasize different information; use discrete points for integer item counts.

column2: (a) Even: f(−x)=f(x), y-axis symmetry; examples x², cos x, abs(x). (b) Odd: f(−x)=−f(x), origin symmetry; examples x, x³, sin x.
column3: For even functions, (x,y) pairs with (−x,y). For odd functions it pairs with (−x,−y). Check each example directly by replacing x with −x.
column4: These identities require a domain symmetric about zero; the zero function satisfies both.

column2: Increasing means f(x1)<f(x2) whenever x1<x2 in the stated interval.
column3: Pick any two inputs in order; the output at the later input must be greater. The graph consequently rises from left to right throughout that interval.
column4: The condition applies to every pair, not just to the interval's endpoints or the graph's net trend.

column2: A mathematical model is a mathematical description of a real situation, often using equations or functions.
column3: For constant speed v, d(t)=vt models travel distance. It identifies variables, assumes fixed speed, predicts distance, and can be checked against measurements.
column4: A model is an idealization; its assumptions and useful input range limit its predictions.

column3: A linear rule has degree 1; a power is x^a; an exponential has variable exponent; a quadratic degree 2; the fifth-degree polynomial's largest power is 5; a rational rule is a quotient of polynomials.
column4: Use the natural real domains: x≥0 for the example fractional power and x≠2 for the example rational function. The examples are not unique.

column2: Sketch x, x², x³, x⁴ together: all pass (0,0),(1,1); even powers are y-axis symmetric, odd powers origin symmetric.
column3: At x=−1 the heights are −1,1,−1,1. For 0<x<1, x>x²>x³>x⁴; for x>1 the order reverses.
column4: These comparisons, plus straightness of y=x and flattening of higher powers near zero, distinguish all four curves without a dense table.

column2: (a) sine wave, amplitude 1 and period 2π; (b) tangent branches with period π and asymptotes π/2+kπ; (c) positive increasing e^x through (0,1); (d) increasing ln x through (1,0), x>0; (e) reciprocal hyperbola in quadrants I and III; (f) V at (0,0); (g) √x from (0,0), x≥0; (h) arctangent sigmoid through 0 with asymptotes ±π/2.
column3: Use zeros and anchor points: sin has zeros kπ; tan has zeros kπ; e^x approaches y=0 to the left; ln has vertical asymptote x=0; 1/x has both coordinate axes as asymptotes; abs(x) has slopes ±1; √x passes (1,1),(4,2).
column4: Keep each function's actual domain. Arctangent has all real inputs, while tangent excludes its asymptote inputs.

column3: Sum and product require both outputs at the same input. The quotient needs those two outputs and a nonzero denominator.
column4: A simplified algebraic rule can appear to have a larger domain; the domain of the original combination still governs.

column3: Evaluate the inner function first, then use its output as the next input. Both evaluations must exist.
column4: The domain is generally not just Df∩Dg, because f is evaluated at g(x), not at x.

column3: For a source point (a,b), translate or scale the appropriate coordinate. In (i), x/2=a gives x=2a; in (j), 2x=a gives x=a/2.
column4: An input multiplier has the reciprocal effect on horizontal coordinates, while an output multiplier acts directly on heights.

column2: (a) One-to-one means equal outputs imply equal inputs; the graph passes the horizontal-line test. (b) f⁻¹(y)=x iff f(x)=y; reflect its graph in y=x.
column3: The inverse swaps every (x,y) to (y,x). One-to-one behavior ensures no two swapped points have the same first coordinate and different heights.
column4: The inverse's domain is the original range and its range is the original domain; it is not 1/f.

column2: (a) arcsin reverses sine on [−π/2,π/2], domain [−1,1], range [−π/2,π/2]. (b) arccos reverses cosine on [0,π], domain [−1,1], range [0,π]. (c) arctan reverses tangent on (−π/2,π/2), domain ℝ, range (−π/2,π/2).
column3: Restrict each periodic forward function to an interval where it is one-to-one and attains its full usual range; interchange that restricted domain and range.
column4: The branch restrictions explain why inverse trigonometric functions return one principal angle rather than every angle with that sine, cosine, or tangent.

column3: Take f(x)=x² and s=t=1. Then f(s+t)=f(2)=4, but f(s)+f(t)=1+1=2.
column4: Function evaluation is not generally distributive over addition.

column3: For f(x)=x², f(1)=f(−1)=1 although 1≠−1.
column4: The implication would be valid if f were assumed one-to-one, which is not stated.

column3: For f(x)=x² and x=1, f(3x)=9 while 3f(x)=3.
column4: Multiplying an input and multiplying an output are different operations.

column3: The definition of a decreasing function is precisely that larger inputs have smaller outputs: x1<x2 implies f(x1)>f(x2).
column4: Use both inputs in the interval on which the function is decreasing.

column3: At a fixed input a, a function has at most the single output f(a), so x=a can intersect its graph at most once.
column4: Inputs outside the domain produce no intersection, which is also allowed by at most once.

column3: Let f(x)=x+1 and g(x)=x². Then f(g(x))=x²+1, but g(f(x))=(x+1)²; they differ, for example, at x=1.
column4: Composition's order matters; equal special examples do not prove a universal identity.

column3: For f(x)=2x, the inverse is f⁻¹(x)=x/2, whereas the reciprocal is 1/(2x). At x=2 these give 1 and 1/4.
column4: The superscript −1 denotes an inverse operation here, not a reciprocal power.

column3: e^x is strictly positive, so it is never a zero denominator.
column4: Positivity of an exponential makes division valid even when it is very small.

column3: ln is strictly increasing on (0,∞), so positive inputs a<b produce ln a<ln b.
column4: The positive-input assumption is necessary for real logarithms.

column3: Choose x=e: (ln e)⁶=1 but 6ln e=6.
column4: The actual power law is ln(x⁶)=6ln x for x>0, not a sixth power of ln x.

column3: With x=a=e, (ln x)/(ln a)=1 but ln(x/a)=ln1=0.
column4: The quotient on the left is log_a x by change of base; subtraction of logarithms, not division, corresponds to a quotient of arguments.

column3: arctan(−1)=−π/4 because this angle lies in (−π/2,π/2). Although tan(3π/4)=−1, 3π/4 is outside arctan's principal range.
column4: An inverse trigonometric function returns the selected principal representative.

column3: At x=1, arctan1=π/4 but arcsin1/arccos1=(π/2)/0 is undefined.
column4: The identity tanθ=sinθ/cosθ cannot be inverted by distributing inverse notation over the quotient.

column3: With x=−1, √(x²)=1≠−1. In general √(x²)=abs(x).
column4: The square-root symbol denotes the nonnegative root.

column3: Read the height at x=2 and crossings with y=3. Project onto the axes for domain/range; the graph rises between its minimum at x=−4 and maximum at x=4. Horizontal lines can cross more than once.
column4: Origin symmetry pairs (x,y) with (−x,−y), establishing oddness. Intermediate readings are estimates from the supplied grid.

column2: (a) g(2)=3; (b) strictly increasing; (c) g⁻¹(2)≈0.3; (d) approximately [−1,3.5]; (e) reflect g across y=x.
column3: Read g at input 2. For the inverse value, find the original input at height 2. For the inverse domain, read the original graph's full vertical extent, from about −1 to 3.5.
column4: The steep middle portion makes a precise inverse estimate difficult; an estimate near 0.3–0.5 is consistent with the graph's scale. Strict increase guarantees an inverse function.

column3: f(a+h)−f(a)=[(a+h)²−2(a+h)+3]−[a²−2a+3]=2ah+h²−2h. Divide by h.
column4: The constants cancel and every remaining term contains h; cancellation is valid only when h is nonzero.

column2: Yield increases at first, then levels off and can decrease when excess fertilizer damages the crop.
column3: Sketch a curve starting at the unfertilized yield, rising to an optimum, then falling for excessive application. Restrict fertilizer amounts and yield to physically meaningful nonnegative values.
column4: There is no unique formula or maximum specified. A monotonically increasing curve forever would ignore possible overfertilization.

column3: For 2/(3x−1), exclude 3x−1=0. The numerator cannot vanish, so y=0 is impossible. For any y≠0, solving y=2/(3x−1) gives x=(1+2/y)/3.
column4: Solving for x proves every nonzero output is attained, rather than merely noting that zero is absent.

column3: √(16−x⁴) requires x⁴≤16, hence abs(x)≤2. Its maximum is 4 at x=0 and minimum 0 at x=±2.
column4: The even fourth power constrains both positive and negative inputs symmetrically.

column3: ln(x+6) requires x+6>0. As x goes from just above −6 to arbitrarily large values, the argument covers (0,∞), so its logarithm covers all reals.
column4: A horizontal translation changes the logarithm's domain, not its range.

column3: Since −1≤cos2t≤1, adding 3 gives 2≤3+cos2t≤4. Both bounds are attained.
column4: The factor 2 changes the period to π, but not the cosine amplitude.

column2: (a) up 8; (b) left 8; (c) vertical stretch ×2, then up 1; (d) right 2 and down 2; (e) reflect in x-axis; (f) reflect in y=x when f is one-to-one.
column3: Track a generic point (a,b): the new points are (a,b+8),(a−8,b),(a,1+2b),(a+2,b−2),(a,−b),(b,a).
column4: The inverse reflection in (f) is different from reflecting in either coordinate axis.

column2: For each source point (a,b), plot (a+8,b), (a,−b), (a,2−b), (a,b/2−1), (b,a), (b−3,a), in order (a)–(f).
column3: Apply each coordinate rule to all visible source-curve points, keeping their order and endpoint inclusion. In (e), swap coordinates to obtain f⁻¹. In (f), then translate that inverse three units left.
column4: The supplied curve is increasing, so its inverse is a function. Coordinate mapping specifies the transformed whole curve rather than merely an isolated sample point.

column2: Cubic y=(x−2)³ with inflection and zero (2,0), domain and range ℝ.
column3: Move y=x³ right two; anchor points become (1,−1),(2,0),(3,1).
column4: The translation occurs inside the cube, so it changes horizontal positions.

column2: y=2√x starts at (0,0), passes (1,2),(4,4), domain [0,∞), range [0,∞).
column3: Double the heights of the standard square-root graph.
column4: Vertical scaling does not change which inputs have real square roots.

column3: Complete the square x²−2x+2=(x−1)²+1, giving a right shift of 1 and upward shift of 1.
column4: No real x-intercepts occur because the squared term plus one is positive.

column2: y=ln(x+1); domain (−1,∞), vertical asymptote x=−1, intercept (0,0).
column3: Shift the natural-log graph one unit left.
column4: The logarithm's argument remains strictly positive; the asymptote is not part of the graph.

column3: Compress cosine horizontally by factor 2 and reflect in the x-axis. One cycle has heights −1,0,1,0,−1 at x=0,π/4,π/2,3π/4,π.
column4: The leading minus reverses the initial peak into a trough without changing the period.

column2: For x<0 draw y=−x; for x≥0 draw y=e^x−1; they meet at (0,0).
column3: The left branch is a descending line toward zero. The right branch starts at e⁰−1=0 and increases exponentially; the full range is [0,∞).
column4: Use only each rule's specified half-line. The value at zero comes from the exponential branch, and both limiting heights agree.

column3: (a) 2x⁵−3x²+2 mixes odd and nonzero even terms. (b) (−x)³−(−x)⁷=−(x³−x⁷). (c) e^(−(−x)²)=e^(−x²). (d) 1+sin(−x)=1−sin x, matching neither the original nor its negative.
column4: Substitute −x and compare complete expressions; a nonzero constant term prevents oddness unless other terms compensate identically.

column3: The segment slope is (0−2)/(−1−(−2))=−2 and its intercept is −2. The upper radius-1 semicircle satisfies x²+y²=1 and y≥0.
column4: The two pieces agree at (−1,0), so assigning that shared endpoint to either or both gives the same function.

column3: Compose f=ln x and g=x²−9 in the requested order. In (a), x²−9 must be positive. In (c), ln x must itself be positive before applying the second log.
column4: The outer logarithm restricts its whole inner output; inner-domain checks cannot be skipped.

column2: h(x)=√x; g(u)=u+√u; f(v)=1/v, so F=f∘g∘h on x>0.
column3: Apply h to get √x, then g to get √x+∜x, then reciprocal to obtain 1/(√x+∜x).
column4: The first two roots permit x≥0, but the final denominator is zero at x=0, so exclude that endpoint.

column2: One reasonable linear model is L(t)≈50.13636364+0.249272727t years, t=year−1900; its 2010 prediction is ≈77.56 years.

column4: The data show changing gains, so other defensible fitted families can give different predictions. This historical-model extrapolation is not a measured 2010 value.
The slope estimates variable cost per extra unit; the intercept estimates fixed weekly cost under the linear assumption.

column4: The inverse value can be identified by forward substitution without a closed-form inverse formula.

column4: The original domain excludes x=−1/2 and the original range excludes y=1/2.
